title: Atrial fibrillation: anticoagulation and rate control

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS atrial fibrillation guideline. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: Which items score two points in CHA2DS2-VASc?
questions.why: Everything else scores one, including age 65 to 74 and vascular disease. The maximum score is nine.

questions.q: At what CHA2DS2-VASc score is anticoagulation recommended for a man with atrial fibrillation?
questions.why: For a woman the threshold is 3, because female sex adds a point without adding much risk on its own. At the score below the threshold, anticoagulation is reasonable rather than recommended.

questions.q: For most patients with atrial fibrillation who need anticoagulation, which is preferred?
questions.why: Aspirin, alone or with clopidogrel, is not recommended for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation; it adds bleeding without matching the benefit.

questions.q: In which patients is warfarin preferred over a direct oral anticoagulant?
questions.why: These are the two settings where the trials of direct agents either excluded patients or showed harm. Everywhere else the direct agents are at least as effective with less intracranial bleeding.

questions.q: Which criteria reduce the apixaban dose to 2.5 mg twice daily when two of them are present?
questions.why: Any two of the three. Under-dosing without meeting the criteria is a common error and leaves patients with more strokes for no bleeding benefit.

questions.q: What is the INR target for warfarin in atrial fibrillation?
questions.why: Time in therapeutic range matters as much as the target; below about 65% is one reason to switch to a direct agent.

questions.q: A patient has a HAS-BLED score of 3. What does that change?
questions.a: Address the modifiable bleeding risks; anticoagulate anyway
questions.why: The score exists to flag blood pressure, alcohol, NSAIDs, labile INR and the like for correction, not to deny anticoagulation to patients whose stroke risk is higher still.

questions.q: For lenient rate control in atrial fibrillation, what resting heart rate is acceptable?
questions.why: Lenient control was as good as strict control for outcomes in trials, so long as symptoms are controlled and ventricular function is preserved.

questions.q: A patient with atrial fibrillation and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction needs rate control. Which class should be avoided?
questions.why: Diltiazem and verapamil depress contractility and worsen HFrEF. Beta blockers are first-line; digoxin is the usual add-on.

questions.q: Atrial fibrillation of more than 48 hours or unknown duration. How long should anticoagulation precede elective cardioversion, unless a transoesophageal echo excludes thrombus?
questions.why: And at least 4 weeks after, regardless of CHA2DS2-VASc, because atrial stunning after cardioversion carries its own thrombus risk.
Andexanet alfa reverses the factor Xa inhibitors; four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate is the usual alternative for them. Vitamin K is for warfarin.

questions.q: A patient with atrial fibrillation and a high stroke risk cannot take long-term anticoagulation. What is the alternative?
questions.why: Ablation reduces symptoms and recurrence but does not remove the need for anticoagulation, which continues by stroke risk score rather than by rhythm.
